title: Owning the Pipe Is Worth More Than Renting It
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0605: Email from Jonathan Bellack to Aparna Pappu et al. (May 10, 2018)
excerptForBlog: Intuitively we know that moving $1 from DBM-3PE to DBM-AdX gets us a 20% revshare we didn't have before, so it should deliver a ton. The bigger question is how to do that, and whether we've tested any. Questions like: is there a defensible way to change DBM buying strategy to move more spend from 3PE to AdX? How much lift do publishers actually get today by calling DBM multiple times through different 3PE, relative to running all of DBM through AdX? Can we build features or set commercial terms that give pubs & buyers more incentive to run DBM through AdX instead of through 3PE? Should we change the DBM buying strategy entirely for emerging businesses like mApp, instead of recreating the Web's 3PE marketplace? We're just starting to pivot toward these questions on the sell side, there's a lot more to do.

lessonTitle: Owning the Pipe Is Worth More Than Renting It
pullQuote: Every dollar that flows through someone else's exchange is a dollar where you don't set the toll — and Bellack's math shows just how big that toll can be.
situation: In May 2018, Google executive Jonathan Bellack wrote internally about a straightforward revenue arithmetic: shifting ad spend from third-party exchanges (3PE) into Google's own AdX exchange would capture a 20% revenue share that Google was otherwise leaving on the table. The email poses a series of concrete questions about how to make that shift happen — through product features, commercial terms, or changed defaults for new business lines.
insight: Bellack isn't discovering a new market. He's identifying a **leakage problem**: money that flows through Google's buy-side tool (DBM) is escaping to third-party exchanges instead of staying inside Google's sell-side (AdX). The 20% revenue share figure makes the stakes concrete — every dollar redirected is a direct margin gain. His questions reveal a classic **vertical integration** instinct: if you own both the buyer and the seller, you want transactions to clear on your own exchange, not a competitor's. He even flags a cleaner path for new products ('emerging businesses like mApp'), suggesting it's easier to set the right defaults from the start than to change existing behavior. The document does not reveal what decisions were ultimately made; it captures the thinking at the start of the pivot.
application: Map your own product's transaction flow. Anywhere a customer journey exits your platform to complete a step — payment, fulfillment, discovery — ask Bellack's question: is there a feature or commercial term that keeps that step inside your ecosystem? Start with new product lines where you set the default, not legacy products where you fight existing habits.
